claim_verdicts.evidence: "A *breakpoint* temporarily interrupts the execution of the application before the line with the breakpoint is run." (:60) and "Program execution stops when it reaches the breakpoint and before the `Console.WriteLine` method executes. The **Locals** window displays the values of variables that are defined in the currently executing method." (:74, repeated for VS Code at :138). The docs scope the displayed values to the running method — see the section 3 issue on the lesson's wider wording.

"Choose **Debug** > **Step Into**. Another way to debug one statement at a time is by pressing F11." (:322) then "Visual Studio highlights and displays an arrow beside the next line of execution." (:324). :330-338 press F11 once per statement, each press executing one statement and refreshing Locals — the run is suspended again after each. The VS Code walkthrough (:360-386) is identical.

"Each time the breakpoint is hit, the debugger calls the `String.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)` method, and it breaks on this line only if the method call returns `true`." (:236) and "Because the condition you specified ... has been satisfied, program execution stops when it reaches the breakpoint and before the `Console.WriteLine` method executes." (:246).

C# reference, `for`: "The *condition* section that determines if the next iteration in the loop should run. If it evaluates to `true` or isn't present, the next iteration runs. Otherwise, the loop exits." — the first evaluation gates the first pass. Ran `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- wrong-total` at stage-0: second line is "one line only: expected 1250000, got 0" (one item, `i < 0` false, body never ran). With claim 1 (break before the marked line runs) a breakpoint in that body is never hit.

WrongTotal.cs at stage-0: :10 `for (var i = 0; i < lines.Count - 1; i++)`, :12 `totalVnd += lines[i].Quantity * lines[i].UnitPriceVnd;`, :20 `{ (1, 1_250_000), (2, 450_000) }` → Count 2, condition `i < 1`, so the body runs once with i = 0. Labelled `opinion` and read as one in the lesson: a judgement about what counts as evidence. No documented behaviour is asserted; the mechanism it rests on (a suspended run shows the values that exist at that line) is claim 1, verified against debug-console-app.md:60, :74.

Opinion, now stated with its conditions, and the hedge the earlier review asked for is present: the branch turns on "a machine you cannot attach to", not on who owns it. That matters because managed-debuggers.md:19 says Visual Studio "can also be used to debug Linux apps running remotely, in WSL, or in Docker containers". Section 4 of the lesson matches the claim ("a machine you cannot hook onto").

Exception.StackTrace "Contains a stack trace that can be used to determine where an error occurred. The stack trace includes the source file name and program line number if debugging information is available." — it is a property of the exception object, so the trace only reaches a reader if the exception goes unhandled or is logged. A caught-and-swallowed exception leaves nothing; both Debug samples return wrong values and print no trace. The claim needs that condition.
claim_verdicts.source: refs/dotnet-docs/docs/standard/exceptions/exception-class-and-properties.md:27; runs of `-- wrong-total` and `-- logging-demo` at stage-0
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Opinion: log the inputs a function received and the decisions it took, with their values, not the bare fact that execution reached a point — where something throws and the trace is surfaced (unhandled, or caught and logged) the trace already names the path, and where nothing throws "got here" carries no value to compare against.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Opinion given with its condition (removed once the question is answered). Its factual half follows from LoggingDemo.cs:8-21: the three WriteLine calls sit inside `TotalVnd`, so every call prints once plus once per pass plus once on return.

Opinion: a judgement about when to attach a condition. The mechanism underneath is verified elsewhere — a breakpoint interrupts execution each time its line is about to run (debug-console-app.md:60), a conditional one "breaks on this line only if the method call returns `true`" (:236).

Opinion: a placement judgement. Its factual half is verified — WrongTotal.cs:12 is the adding statement inside the body and :10 is the `for` statement; with a one-item order the body never runs (run output "one line only: expected 1250000, got 0"), so a breakpoint in the body is never hit and the silence is the answer.

Exception.StackTrace "Contains a stack trace that can be used to determine where an error occurred. The stack trace includes the source file name and program line number if debugging information is available." The repo's captured trace shows the parameter, not the value: "ArgumentNullException: Value cannot be null. (Parameter 's')". ArgumentOutOfRangeException: "The ParamName property identifies the invalid argument, and the ActualValue property, if a value is present, identifies the invalid value"; ActualValue "Gets the argument value that causes this exception."

Right for every case the lesson uses, wrong at the edge: LoggingDemo.cs prints once at :10, once per pass at :16 and once at :19, and `i < lines.Count - 1` runs the body n-1 times, so the count is 1 + (n-1) + 1 = n + 1 only for n ≥ 1. For an empty list the loop body never runs and the function still prints the two lines outside it, i.e. 2 lines where n + 1 = 1. Observed for n = 2: exactly the three lines of claim 8.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang stage-0: LoggingDemo.cs:10, 13, 16, 19, 24; `dotnet run -- logging-demo`, dotnet SDK 10
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: LoggingDemo.TotalVnd writes one call line, one line per loop pass and one return line, so an order of n ≥ 1 items prints n + 1 lines: three for the two-item order, four for a three-item one (an empty list prints the two lines outside the loop).

claim_verdicts.evidence: A breakpoint "temporarily interrupts the execution of the application before the line with the breakpoint is run" (:60) — it interrupts at marked lines only, and continuing is not stepping: ":180 Press F5 to continue program execution" is followed by the program's output and "Press any key to exit the application and stop debugging", i.e. the run went on unstopped. With claim 5's single hit at i = 0, `i` becomes 1, `i < 1` is false and the method returns; no other line is marked, so reaching `return` needs a step.

"Set a *breakpoint* on the line that displays the name, date, and time, by clicking in the left margin of the code window on that line. The left margin is to the left of the line numbers." (:64, same wording for VS Code at :88) then "Press F5 to run the program in Debug mode. Another way to start debugging is by choosing **Debug** > **Start Debugging** from the menu." (:70). What is absent from the sample is a line announcing entry and nothing else. Claim 10 covers what the three lines contain; nothing in the ledger supports "no line announces that the function was entered".

issues.text: Wider than claim 1 ("the values of the variables in scope") and than the pinned docs, which say the Locals/Variables window "displays the values of variables that are defined in the currently executing method" (debug-console-app.md:74). A line can also use a static field or another object's property, and those are not in that window. True of this loop, where `i`, `totalVnd` and `lines` are all locals or parameters; overstated as a definition. The same words recur in quiz q1's `correct` explanation and q2 option b's explanation.
issues.quote: hands you every variable that line could use
issues.fix: In section 3 write "...and hands you the values of the variables the running method holds — for this loop `i`, `totalVnd` and `lines`." Use the same wording where the phrase recurs: q1 `correct` and q2 option b explanations (en + vi).

issues.text: Holds only when the trace is surfaced. Per the pinned docs the stack trace is a property of the exception object ("Contains a stack trace that can be used to determine where an error occurred"), so it reaches a reader only if the exception goes unhandled or is logged; an exception caught and swallowed leaves no trace at all — exactly the case where a log line is the only record left of an unattended run. As written it tells a junior that throwing code never needs a log line.
issues.quote: a run that throws already has a stack trace naming the path
issues.fix: Write "a run that throws and leaves its trace behind already names the path". Apply the same condition to claim 15 in .meta.json, whose suggested_text is given in this review.

issues.text: Unconditional "never" in summary line 4, while section 4 states the condition that carries it (where something throws, the trace already names the path). The pinned .NET docs prescribe nothing about which lines to log, so the absolute is the author's rule presented as a law, and it is the line a reader memorises.
issues.quote: never the bare fact that the code reached a point
issues.fix: Write summary line 4 as "Log the inputs a function received and the decisions it took; a line saying only that the code reached a point costs a reader and returns nothing."
